Would students benefit from being able to attend classes from home?

The American Education System has grown a lot since it was originally curated. While I do believe there have been positives to have come from today's educational system, I also believe there are improvements that can be made. One important improvement would be the ability to attend classes online. I believe students would benefit very well from attending classes from home, due to the style of today's stress-inducing form of schooling.

First of all, this would be very beneficial because attending classes from home would help relieve stress from students with social anxieties or anxieties involving the typical school format. The stress levels of students has grown exponentially in the passed couple of decades, and I've seen it first hand. Students are growing more and more anxious as the expectations to get good grades, get into a good school, and follow a career in STEM become higher. How are we to expect our students handle these sort of worries while also trying to balance a social life? My younger sister has aspired to be many things; including a doctor, a biologist, and even a detective. But do to her hyper-thyroidism she has been held back by her medical testings and re-diagnosis' during the school year. This has caused an immense amount of stress and anxiety--but after many meetings and emails between my parents and the school, she was accommodated with home bound. Home bound is a form of at-home schooling that allows her to take some classes from home and work with teachers outside of school hours in order to help her get caught up.

Second of all, attending classes from home would allow for more flexibility when it comes to the scheduling of classes, and potentially assignment deadlines. If a student struggles to balance school, extra-curricular activities, and a job, they would probably find online classes to be very beneficial. When taking classes online, students are usually allowed for more freedom and flexibility. They can sleep in until noon, and then work on a class in the evening. Or if they work to help support their family, they can get up early, get their school work done, and work a job in the afternoon. Most online classes are scheduled similarly to college courses, and will allow students to plan when during the week they wish to take certain classes. My younger sister, who I spoke of earlier, has found this to be very beneficial, and something she will miss once she can fully reimmerse herself into a regular school schedule.

Lastly, attending classes from home would allow for more involvement of the parent in the students education. Some parents do not get a full scope of what is going on in a students school day, and it can sometimes be hard for kids to communicate this to their parents. Some parents tend to job the gun when they take a look at their grades and are seeing their kid isn't doing too well, but what they aren't always considering is the other factors that go into it. A students grade could be reflective of not only their work ethic and focus, but how well a teacher is teaching them, and the sort relationships between other kids in the class. If a parent is able to be present when a student is working on their courses, they would be able to get a full scope of how their student learns. Not only that, but the student would have less distractions from other kids, and hopefully be able to avoid some of the flaws of an individual teachers style of teaching.

Now while I do believe others would combat my claim with statements such as, "today's educational system has done amazing and has left many students with successful careers in medicine and engineering". But to that I would say; there have also been many successful people in history such as scientist, Albert Einstein and entrepreneur, Gary Vee, who either dropped out of high school or didn't find themselves doing so great until university. That is why I believe students would benefit very well from attending classes from home, to help relieve the stress of today's school system.

Subject: In Support of Retaining the Electoral College

Dear [State Senator's Name],

I hope this letter finds you well. I am writing to express my support for retaining the Electoral College as the method of electing the President of the United States. While some argue for a change to a popular vote system, I believe that the Electoral College is a vital and necessary component of our democratic process. In this letter, I will present several reasons based on the information provided in the passages to support my claim.

One of the key advantages of the Electoral College system is the certainty of outcome it provides. As we have seen in previous elections, the winning candidate's share of the electoral votes often exceeds their share of the popular vote. This serves to create a clear and decisive victory, reducing the likelihood of disputes over the election results (Posner, 18). Furthermore, the winner-take-all method employed by most states ensures that even a slight plurality in a state leads to a landslide electoral-vote victory, making ties in the nationwide electoral vote highly improbable (Posner, 18).

Another important advantage of the Electoral College is that it ensures that the president is a representative of the entire nation and not just certain regions. Candidates must have trans-regional appeal to secure enough electoral votes for victory. This prevents candidates from solely focusing on winning the popular vote in specific regions, which may result in a president who only prioritizes the interests of a specific area while disregarding others (Posner, 19). By requiring candidates to appeal to a diverse range of states, the Electoral College ensures that the president is genuinely "everyone's president."

The Electoral College also encourages candidates to campaign in swing states, which are instrumental in deciding the election outcomes. Swing states receive significant attention, as candidates recognize the importance of winning their electoral votes. This mechanism compels candidates to engage with voters in these states, resulting in more informed and thoughtful voters who play a decisive role in the election (Posner, 20). This focus on swing states leads to a more competitive and engaging electoral process.

Furthermore, the Electoral College restores balance to the political power held by large and small states. While the mal-apportionment of the Senate may result in a disparity in the political influence of states, the Electoral College ensures that candidates pay attention to both large and small states during their campaigns. In this way, the Electoral College offsets the potential imbalance caused by the Senate's structure, ensuring that states of all sizes have their concerns and interests addressed by presidential candidates (Posner, 21).

Lastly, the Electoral College avoids the need for run-off elections when no candidate receives a majority of the popular vote. This eliminates the potential complications and additional expenses associated with such elections. Instead, the Electoral College consistently produces a clear winner with a majority of electoral votes, thus maintaining stability in the election process (Posner, 22).

While some critics argue that the Electoral College discourages voters in states where their preferred candidate has little chance of winning, it should be noted that voter participation remains high despite this factor (Posner, 23). Voters are motivated to express their political preferences, even if they understand that their vote may not swing a national election. The high turnout in presidential elections demonstrates a continued commitment to participating in the democratic process.

In conclusion, the Electoral College plays a crucial role in our democratic system of electing the President of the United States. It provides certainty of outcomes, ensures a president who represents the entire nation, encourages candidates to campaign in swing states, balances the influence of large and small states, and eliminates the need for run-off elections. These advantages outweigh the arguments for changing to a popular vote system. I respectfully urge you to support the retention of the Electoral College in our electoral process.

Thank you for considering my perspective. I look forward to your continued dedication to representing the interests of our state and our nation.

Sincerely,

The United States is a car-centric country. We have built our cities and our lifestyles around the idea that everyone needs a car to get around. But this is not sustainable. Third, cars are a major source of traffic congestion. Traffic jams waste time and fuel, and they make it difficult to get around.

There are many things we can do to limit car usage. One is to build more public transportation. This will give people more options for getting around without a car. Another is to make it easier to walk and bike. This can be done by building more sidewalks and bike lanes. We can also make it more expensive to drive by raising the price of gas and parking.

* Improved air quality: Cars are a major source of air pollution. They emit exhaust fumes that contain harmful pollutants, such as carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, and particulate matter. * Reduced traffic congestion: Cars are also a major source of traffic congestion. Traffic jams waste time and fuel, and they make it difficult to get around. Limiting car usage will help to reduce traffic congestion and make it easier to get around.
* Saved money: Driving is expensive. The initial purchase price of a car is high, but so are the costs of gas, insurance, and maintenance. Limiting car usage will help to save money on these costs.
* More livable cities: Cars make cities less livable. They create noise pollution, they take up valuable space, and they make it difficult to walk or bike. Limiting car usage will make cities more livable and more enjoyable for everyone.

Drivers Should Not Use Cell Phones in Any Capacity While Driving

In today's world, cell phones have become remarkably integrated into our daily lives. However, using a cell phone while driving can be extremely dangerous and should be avoided. There are several reasons why drivers should not be allowed to use cell phones in any capacity when operating a vehicle. 

First and foremost, cell phone use significantly increases accident risks. Numerous scientific studies have found that drivers who use cell phones are much more likely to get into crashes serious enough to injure themselves or others. This is because cell phones demand attention that should be focused on the road instead. Even hands-free usage impairs concentration and awareness of surroundings. 

Secondly, cell phone conversations and other distractions greatly reduce reaction time needed in emergency road situations. A driver's hands should remain on the wheel and their eyes on the road ahead to anticipate and respond to potential hazards like suddenly stopped traffic. Texting or talking ties up both mental and physical faculties better dedicated to safe vehicle operation. Reaction times are noticeably slower when the mind is split between phone and road.

In addition, cell phone involvements undermine traffic laws. Drivers on cell phones are prone to speeding, ignoring signs/signals, drifting between lanes, tailgating and other violations arising from lack of attentiveness. Not only does this endanger themselves, but puts everyone sharing the road at risk of harm from reckless behavior. Allowing phones permissions counteracts the cooperative regulations in place to structure orderly and safe transportation. 

In summary, cell phone technology should not come at the cost of human lives lost to preventable accidents. Individual convenience is outweighed by collective safety on public roads. Stricter laws banning all cell phone handling behind the wheel aim to deter deadly distractions and curb the significant risks of multi-tasking phones with multi-ton vehicles. For the protection of all citizens on the road, drivers' full focus must remain with traffic, not telecommunications, while in control of motion machinery.

As with many students, receiving an education and taking classes is associated with a physical school building. Students are often aware of the two main options for school: attending public/private institutions or home school. Each option offers different advantages and disadvantages but seem to be on opposite sides of a continuum. The option of taking online classes provide the benefits of both attending an in person school and home school. It can be seen as a middle ground on the continuum as taking online classes in addition to regular classes at school may increase learning. Distance learning benefits students as it can enhance learning, provide a more comfortable environment, and give students the opportunity to take classes not offered at school.

Online learning can be beneficial to students who have a different learning style. They tend to be more heavily technology based which can enhance learning of those who thrive on more technology incorporated lessons and assignments. Because classes are taken online, the teacher or instructor utilizes different technological tools and resources for lesson plan and activities. It broadens the possibilities of how information can be delivered to students and the different class work students can participate in. Online classes can also seem a more appealing option to in person classes, as lessons and assignments tend to be more direct and straight forward. Often times, school teachers give "fluff" assignments that don't necessarily have a purpose or that don't offer much learning potential. These assignments are given to pass time and give students an activity to do whether in class or for homework. I have endured my share of "fluff" assignments throughout high school. During my sophomore year, I despised English class because I didn't seem to gain anything out of it. My teacher would assign miscellaneous assignments such as a food poem or a repetitive packet of work. Online classes tend to include less of these "fluff" assignments because they differ from traditional in person classes where students meet personally with teachers. There is less of a worry to keep students occupied with different assignments each class. With the Generic_School Online Campus, students are given assignments to complete each week with the due date at the end of that week. Teachers tend to give less unnecessary assignments because the class can be more spread out throughout the course.

Taking online classes from home provides students with a more comfortable learning environment. They are in the comforts of their home and have the freedom to attain food or use the bathroom at any given time. Video conferences can be held once a week and may not even reveal a student's appearance, so students can wear whatever clothing they desire or feel most comfortable in. Students are not in the high stress school environment and can feel more relaxed. This may lead to an increase in productivity and focus on one's schoolwork. Although some students lack a healthy domestic environment, online classes are an additional option for students to take. Many students enjoy taking traditional in person school classes because they can escape an unhealthy or distracting home environment, but distance learning simply exists as an additional option for students to take advantage of. Students can choose to take online classes or not depending on their situation and preference. While some students have distracting homes, other students can benefit from online classes as it may provide a quiet and less distracting atmosphere. Students tend to get distracted by classmates at school, so online classes may increase productivity as students can focus more on their work.

The classes offered at each school varies. Students may want to enroll in a specific class but there can be a wait list due to the popularity of the class or it may not be offered at the school. Distance learning allows students the opportunity to take classes which would otherwise not be available. At Generic_School, AP Latin is not a guaranteed class every year. It is entirely dependent on the amount of students who express interest in the class and sign up. When scheduling classes for next year, I requested to take AP Latin, however, if the class will not be available, I will take the class online. With this option of taking online classes, my education will not be hindered or limited. Students should have the opportunity to take whichever class they wish without any restrictions or limitations. Distance learning effectively prevents this situation from occurring with the availability and different offerings of classes.

The argument can be made that attending classes from home does not allow students to develop communication and social skills because of the decrease in social interaction. However, students can develop and hone these skills with continuing to take in person classes at school. Online classes can be taken in addition or in combination with traditional classes at school. Distance learning can enhance education, increase productivity with its more comfortable environment, and expand course selection opportunities for students, but online classes still remain an additional option for students. Students extremely benefit from online classes. Schools must promote and encourage students to take online classes or at the very least, ensure students are aware of this opportunity as an alternative to in person classes. Distance learning provides numerous benefits, and students who take advantage of online classes will have a more enriched education experience.

Limiting car usage can have numerous advantages for both individuals and the environment. By reducing the number of cars on the road, we can make a significant impact in combatting climate change and reducing our carbon footprint.

By reducing car usage, we can reduce the amount of pollution in the air, leading to cleaner and healthier environments.

First impressions are often difficult to change because people tend to form their opinions based on initial observations, which can be influenced by a variety of factors such as appearance, behavior, and body language. As a result, people may not always have an accurate understanding of someone's true character or abilities.

One of the main reasons why first impressions are hard to change is that people often make assumptions based on what they see. For example, a person may assume that another person is not intelligent based on their appearance, even if that person is actually very smart. This can be especially challenging in situations where people are judged based on their appearance, such as in the workplace or in social settings.

Additionally, people may be reluctant to change their first impressions because they want to hold onto their opinions, even if they are not based on accurate information. This can be especially true if the person has formed a negative first impression, as they may be hesitant to let go of that opinion and give the other person a chance to prove themselves.

However, it is possible to change first impressions if people are willing to put in the effort to get to know someone better. For example, if a person has formed a negative first impression of someone based on their appearance, they may be able to change that impression by getting to know the person better and learning more about their personality and interests.

It is also important to be aware of the potential biases that can influence first impressions. For example, people may be more likely to form negative first impressions of people from certain backgrounds or cultures, even if they have never met them before. By being aware of these biases and actively working to overcome them, people can form more accurate and positive first impressions of others.

In conclusion, while first impressions can be difficult to change, it is possible to do so if people are willing to put in the effort to get to know someone better and be aware of their own biases. By doing so, people can form more accurate and positive first impressions of others, which can lead to better relationships and more positive interactions in the future.

As fellow citizens, we must take the necessary steps to preserve our environment and improve our way of life. One of the ways we can do this is by limiting car usage. This means that we should use alternative modes of transportation such as walking, cycling, or using public transport. There are several advantages of limiting car usage and it is important for us to understand them.

Firstly, limiting car usage can help to reduce air pollution in our cities. Cars are one of the major contributors to air pollution as they release harmful gases like carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides. These gases can cause serious health problems such as respiratory diseases, heart attacks, and other cardiovascular diseases. By using alternative modes of transportation, we can significantly reduce the amount of toxic gases released into the air thereby reducing air pollution.

Secondly, using alternative modes of transportation such as cycling or walking can also help to improve our physical health and well-being. It is widely known that regular exercise is essential for maintaining good health. Walking or cycling to work or to the shops can help us to achieve our daily exercise requirements. It can also help to reduce stress levels and improve mental health.

Thirdly, limiting car usage can significantly reduce traffic congestion in our cities. Traffic congestion can lead to increased travel times, wasted fuel, and increased carbon emissions. By using alternative modes of transportation or carpooling, we can reduce the number of cars on the road thereby reducing traffic congestion.

In addition to these benefits, limiting car usage can also help to reduce the amount of money spent on fuel and maintaining cars. Using alternative modes of transportation can be cheaper and can help us save money in the long run.

In conclusion, limiting car usage has numerous advantages for both individuals and the community. It can help to reduce air pollution, improve physical and mental health, reduce traffic congestion, and save money. It is important that we take the necessary steps to reduce car usage and use alternative modes of transportation to help preserve our environment and improve our lifestyle.

One possible solution to this problem is to shorten the length of the school day and add more elective classes. These classes can provide students with a break from the rigid structure of the regular school day and give them the opportunity to explore their passions. Additionally, electives can help students develop new skills and interests that can benefit them in the long run.

Additionally, some students may not have access to elective classes or tutorials if they do not have the resources or support at home.

In conclusion, while there are both pros and cons to changing the typical school day, I believe that it is important to consider the needs and interests of individual students. Why summer projects should be student-designed

The sun is shining, there is a slight breeze in the air, and no one is wearing pants that go past their knees. These are all signs that summer break has officially started. Summer break is the time that all students look forward to, as it means that there aren't any more tests to take and homework to complete. It's a time when students can finally have the opportunity to have fun with family and friends without having to worry about academic stress. However, there are some schools that require students to complete summer projects in order for learning to continue during their break. With this, the question that arises is whether schools should make the teacher design the projects or allow for the projects to be student-designed. These summer projects should be student-designed because it gives students the opportunity to develop research skills, choose topics that they find interesting, and result in an increase in positive mental health.

To begin with, summer projects should be student-designed because it gives students the opportunity to develop research skills. Suppose a teacher assigns a project with specific guidelines and one topic to develop a solution to. This may make the expectations for the student clear-cut, but this type of project learning limits students in what they can explore. With the ability to design your own project, students learn how to research various topics before deciding on the one they will come up with a project to. Not only does this contribute to the development of enhanced research skills among students, but it prepares them for research in the future. In pursuing higher levels of education, it is crucial that students are knowledgeable on how to research about topics efficiently and accurately. Thus, those research skills are developed from student-designed projects and they benefit current and future educational advancement.

Furthermore, summer projects should be student-designed because it gives students the opportunity to choose topics they find interesting. For example, when I was in 6th grade I had a summer project of choosing an influential president and explaining what that president did for the country. At the time, I was interested in science instead of history. As a result, this project seemed lackluster and an arduous task to complete over my summer break. However, if I had been given the opportunity to choose a topic that interests me, I would have found the summer project exponentially more exciting and something to look forward to. Many students feel the same way about this, as they wish to choose the topic they will research and create a solution to. Therefore, it is evident that summer projects should be student-designed so that students can have a genuine interest in the project they are completing.

Lastly, summer projects should be student-designed because it results in an increase in positive mental health. Time and time again summer projects are dreaded by students and a task that many do not look forward to. As a result, students are left unhappy during summer break in regards to completing a project their teacher designed. This is either because the project has limitations, is about an uninteresting topic, or is difficult to complete. These factors can leave students feeling demoralized from completing their summer project and can make summer break a dreary time. Despite these conditions that come with teacher-designed projects, these problems can be solved with student-designed projects. When given the chance to explore what interests you and choosing whether any limitations exist regarding your project, inevitably students are inclined to complete summer projects. From the perspective of a student, you have more motivation to work on a self-designed project. This increased motivation correlates to an increase in mental health. When regarding this benefit, summer projects should be student-designed.

Summer is the time to relax and unwind from the stresses of the school year. It's a time of mornings spent sleeping in, afternoons laying out by the pool, and nights sleeping on the roof, counting the stars that gleam in the sky. That is why students look forward to summer break. As a result, schools should not contribute in reversing the association students make between summer break and enjoyment by assigning teacher-designed projects. With the intention of continual learning occurring over summer break, schools should allow projects to be student-designed. It gives students the chance to explore their passions and make new discoveries without any limitations. Teacher-designed projects only serve in holding students back from doing projects that truly hold meaning to them. Taking into consideration all of these factors, the most logical decision schools can make is having summer projects that are student-designed. This will allow students to have a good time in both the academic and non-academic part of their summer break.

I am writing to you today to express my concern about the Electoral College and its role in electing the President of the United States. As a high school student, I am deeply invested in the future of our country, and I believe that the Electoral College is a system that is outdated and no longer represents the will of the people.

The Electoral College is a system in which each state is allocated a number of electors equal to its number of senators and representatives in Congress. These electors are then responsible for casting their votes for President. The candidate who receives a majority of electoral votes is elected President, even if they did not receive a majority of the popular vote.

This system was created in the 18th century, when the United States was a much smaller country with a much smaller population. It was designed to give smaller states a greater voice in the presidential election, as they would otherwise be overshadowed by the larger states. However, in today's world, the Electoral College is no longer necessary.

The United States is now a much more populous country, and the gap between the population of the largest and smallest states is much smaller. In fact, the smallest state, Wyoming, has a population of just over 500,000 people, while the largest state, California, has a population of over 39 million people. This means that a Wyoming voter has over 66 times the voting power of a California voter.

By 2040, California is expected to have a population of over 50 million people, while Wyoming is expected to have a population of just over 600,000 people. This means that a Wyoming voter will have over 83 times the voting power of a California voter.

This is not fair, and it is not democratic. The Electoral College is a system that disenfranchises voters in large states and gives disproportionate power to voters in small states. This is a system that needs to be changed.

I urge you to support a change to the Electoral College. We need a system that is fair and democratic, and that represents the will of the people.

The Benefits of Limiting Car Usage  

Many communities throughout the world are becoming increasingly dependent on cars for transportation. However, there are advantages to curbing overreliance on personal vehicles. Limiting car usage can both benefit the environment and improve quality of life.

One of the major upsides of restricting car travel is that it leads to reduced pollution and emissions. According to a study conducted in London, decreasing private car journeys by just 10% would cut transport greenhouse gas emissions by over 200,000 tons per year (Source 1). When fewer motor vehicles are on the road, there is less fossil fuel burned and less pollution emitted into the air. This lowers health and environmental costs associated with vehicle emissions. 

In addition, restricting car usage encourages active transportation methods like walking, cycling, and public transit. A report from Vancouver found that residents drove 30% less after the city made infrastructure improvements for cyclists and pedestrians (Source 2). Shifting modes of travel in this way delivers public health gains. Regular physical activity like biking or walking to destinations can help reduce rates of lifestyle diseases. It also makes communities more vibrant as more people experience their neighborhoods by foot rather than from behind the windshield.

Finally, limiting personal cars means less traffic congestion and demand for parking. Source 3 notes that in Manhattan, where alternatives to driving are readily available, traffic moves faster despite having more people and activity compared to car-dependent cities. With fewer vehicles clogging up limited street space, commuters benefit from reduced travel times whether using public transit, walking, biking, or driving. This saves costs associated with time lost in traffic as well as expenses to build additional roadway and parking infrastructure.

In conclusion, curbing overreliance on personal cars produces environmental, public health, and quality of life advantages for communities. Restricting car usage encourages sustainable transportation methods and a more efficient use of limited urban space. By informing citizens about these benefits, more supportive policies can be enacted to realize these gains.

Standardized testing has been a controversial topic in the educational system for a long time. While some people argue that it is an effective way to measure student ability, others claim that it is not an accurate representation of a student's true potential. As a high school student, I believe that standardized tests are not a reliable measure of student ability.

Firstly, standardized tests are often biased towards students from privileged backgrounds. These tests are designed to favor students who have access to quality education, resources, and test preparation. This means that students from low-income families, who may not have the same opportunities, are at a disadvantage. For instance, a study by the National Center for Fair & Open Testing found that students from wealthy families scored higher on the SAT than those from poor families. This shows that standardized tests are not a level playing field, and therefore, cannot accurately measure a student's ability.

Secondly, standardized tests only measure a narrow aspect of intelligence. These tests focus primarily on multiple-choice questions that assess a student's memory and problem-solving skills. However, there are many other important aspects of intelligence that are not taken into account. For example, creativity, critical thinking, and collaboration are essential skills that are not measured by standardized tests. This means that students who excel in these areas may not perform well on the tests, even though they may be highly intelligent and capable.

Furthermore, standardized tests create a culture of test-preparation rather than genuine learning. Teachers and schools often focus on preparing students for the tests, rather than providing a well-rounded education. This can lead to a narrow curriculum that only covers material that is relevant to the tests. As a result, students may not develop a deep understanding of the subject matter, and may not be prepared for the challenges of the real world.

Lastly, the pressure to perform well on standardized tests can have a negative impact on students' mental health. The high stakes associated with these tests can cause students to feel anxious and stressed, which can affect their performance. According to a study by the American Psychological Association, high levels of stress can lead to decreased cognitive function, including memory and problem-solving skills. This means that students who are otherwise capable may not perform well on the tests due to the pressure to succeed.

In conclusion, while standardized tests may seem like an effective way to measure student ability, they are not a reliable measure. These tests are biased towards students from privileged backgrounds, only measure a narrow aspect of intelligence, create a culture of test-preparation rather than genuine learning, and can have a negative impact on students' mental health. Instead of relying solely on standardized tests, schools should focus on providing a well-rounded education that prepares students for the challenges of the real world. This can include project-based learning, experiential education, and assessments that measure a broader range of skills and abilities. By doing so, we can create a more equitable and effective educational system that truly supports the development of all students.

I disagree with the principal's decision to require all students to participate in at least one extracurricular activity. While extracurriculars provide many benefits, mandatory participation should not be imposed on students.

Requiring extracurricular participation leaves no room for student choice or personal circumstances. Not all students have the time or interest to commit to a regular weekly schedule outside of classes. Some may have jobs, family obligations or prefer using their free hours for rest, study or personal hobbies instead. Forcing involvement denies students autonomy over how they spend their non-school hours. 

Extracurriculars are best chosen voluntarily according to personal fit and passion. When compelled to participate, students may resent the lack of choice or feel frustrated by an unsatisfying activity. Forced involvement is unlikely to cultivate long-term enthusiasm or commitment. Students are more likely to gain from extracurriculars if they engage in them of their own free will based on natural motivation and skill alignment. 

A mandate also fails to accommodate diversity of needs, talents and commitments across the student body. One size does not fit all. Some students may already have ample enrichment from other responsibilities or independent pursuits. For others, extracurricular pressures may add undue stress and work overload if not truly interesting to them. A policy of choice allows each student situation and strengths to be respected.

Rather than require across-the-board participation, the principal's goal of student well-being and involvement would be better achieved by promoting extracurricular options and encouraging voluntary involvement. Students who do wish to participate will do so freely, gaining the intended benefits, while others' freedom and circumstances remain accommodated too. Mandating loses these advantages of choice. Overall, student autonomy and diversity of needs counsel against an imposed extracurricular participation rule for all.

Some may feel more comfortable contributing in other ways, such as volunteering or tutoring fellow students. 

Rather than mandating involvement, the principal could encourage participation by promoting opportunities and their benefits. Recognizing student accomplishments, like academic or community service awards, could also motivate engagement. Those who are interested but unable to commit fully could have the option for limited, part-time roles. Ultimately, extracurricular activities should remain voluntary so that each student can structure non-academic time in a manner that works best for their goals and lifestyle. Forcing the issue takes a “one-size-fits-all” approach that is neither practical nor considerate of individual differences.

In conclusion, while extracurriculars offer value, a student's high school experience should not hinge on compulsory activities. Students deserve autonomy over their schedules outside the classroom. The principal's intention to involve the whole student body is understandable but misguided. A policy of obligation could have counterproductive outcomes and fails to respect student priorities and limitations. It is better to encourage engagement through incentives and flexibility than deprive students of personal choice.

I disagree with the principal's decision that all students must participate in at least one extracurricular activity. While extracurriculars provide many benefits, mandatory participation should not be required for several reasons.

First, not all students have the time or ability to take on extra responsibilities outside of school. Some students need to focus their energy on academics in order to maintain good grades. They may have limited time due to other commitments like caring for family members, or jobs to help support the household. Forcing involvement could negatively impact their studies. 

Second, extracurriculars will not appeal equally to all personalities and interests. A shy student may feel anxious being forced to join a sports team or public club. When participation is mandatory, it removes students' freedom to choose activities that truly motivate and engage them. This could diminish the fun and rewards of volunteering. For the activity to be meaningful, involvement should stem from personal choice.

Third, some students may have physical or health issues preventing them from joining certain sports or clubs. A mandatory policy fails to consider these individual circumstances. It does not make accommodations for disabilities or special needs. This type of one-size-fits-all approach can have unintended adverse consequences for vulnerable populations. 

While extracurriculars provide benefits like learning time management, teamwork skills and networking opportunities, students should have autonomy in deciding how they spend their non-academic hours. A better approach is encouraging involvement through informational sessions highlighting the programs available. This empowers students to self-select activities that align with their capabilities and interests, enhancing the experience for all. Overall, requiring participation removes important choices from students and does not account for differences in priorities or abilities. A voluntary system is fairer and allows each individual to tailor involvement in a personally meaningful way.

Imagine learning everything from chemistry to world history at home on a computer screen. Some schools offer distance learning as an option for students to attend classes from home by way of online or video conferencing. Students would be assigned homework, classwork, quizzes, and tests all from an online instructor. Instead of learning in a normal classroom setting, students would watch videos of their teacher or read online notes. If students attended every class at home it would not be beneficial because students who were less indpendent may slack off and they wouldn't be exposed to the social factors that come from attending a regular school.

Many students struggle to pay attention in class or they do not have a very strong work ethic so it's important that they have a teacher there to push them. If they were given the opportunity to attend classes through a computer screen their bad habits may become worse. At home students can be distracted by other screens, younger siblings, pets, and many other things. Attending a normal school limits the amount of distractions a student would face at home. When a student begins to lose focus a teacher is there to remind them to finish their work. However, at home the student may not have someone hovering over their shoulder to make sure that they are absorbing the content.

Also, online schoolong limits the amount of exposure students would have to social situations. In elementary school, students learn more than just spelling and fractions but social skills as well. If a first grader were to take classes online they wouldn't understand how to raise their hand, wait their turn, or share their markers because it would be just them and a screen. In middle school, students would miss out on navigating busy hallways and playing a sport for their school. In high school, they wouldn't be able to participate in honor societies, clubs, or hands on classes. Many students take architecture, film, art, and agriculture classes to discover what they want to do after high school. However, each of these classes require hands on, expensive equipment that most students wouldn't have at home. Online schooling would limit the type of classes a student could take. In addition, many exploratory classes require students to work in teams to solve problems and work on projects. Online schooling would hinder a student's ability to work collaboratively.

Some may argue that online schooling is a better option for students who like to work at their own pace. Some students take a longer time to digest content than others so having their classes online would allow them to spend more time on areas that they struggle with. In a classroom setting, if a single student was struggling but the rest of the class understood the teacher would likely move on. In the same way, online schooling would allow students who move at a faster pace to breeze through material that comes naturally to them. Overall, online schooling would allow students to tailor the pace of their classes to what benefits them best.

In conclusion, online schooling may prevent students from finishing their work and learning the necessary social skills however it would allow them to work at their own pace. Students who are less driven may fall behind in their work because online schooling wouldn't provide any reprecussions. Additionally, students wouldn't benefity from the social situations that come from attending a regular school. Lastly, students would be able to determine the pace of their classes instead of relying on the levels of the students surrounding them in a classroom setting. Online schooling has some benefits however attending a regular school would be more beneficial especially during the developmental stages of a child's life.

While summer is a time meant for rest and relaxation, having some structured learning over the break can help students retain knowledge and develop skills. When it comes to assigning summer projects, I believe giving students some choice and autonomy in designing their own projects strikes the best balance.

Student-designed projects allow individuals to pursue topics that genuinely interest them. This makes the work feel less like a chore and more like an engaging way to spend free time. If students had control over their project topics, they would be intrinsically motivated to dive deeply into learning something new. They could choose to further explore a subject already studied during the school year or investigate an area completely outside the usual curriculum. Having this freedom and control over their education empowers students.

However, teacher guidance is still important to ensure projects have educational merit. Teachers could provide parameters for project scope and content to keep students on track. They could also approve topic ideas to steer clear of subjects inappropriate for schoolwork. With teacher approval of the overall concept, students then scope and carry out the project themselves. This provides structure while still giving independence. 

Student choice also fosters responsibility. By designing their own project guidelines and deadlines, students face real consequences if they fail to follow through. This mimics the independent work environment in college and careers. Meeting self-imposed expectations and staying on schedule for a self-designed project builds important time management skills.

In conclusion, the best summer project system balances student freedom and teacher oversight. Allowing students to choose their own topics within school-approved guidelines empowers independent learning. It also cultivates motivation, responsibility and real-world skills that will serve students well in their educational careers and beyond.

Dear Senator,

I am writing to you today to urge you to support a national popular vote amendment to the United States Constitution. The Electoral College is an outdated and undemocratic system that has no place in our 21st century democracy.

The Electoral College was established in 1787 at the Constitutional Convention. At the time, the Founding Fathers were concerned that a direct election of the president would be too susceptible to fraud and manipulation. They also believed that the Electoral College would provide a more balanced system of representation, giving smaller states a voice in the presidential election.

However, the Electoral College has become increasingly out of step with the needs of our modern democracy. In recent years, there have been several instances in which the candidate who won the popular vote lost the election. This has happened most recently in the 2000 and 2016 elections.

In 2000, Al Gore won the popular vote by over 500,000 votes, but he lost the election to George W. Bush because he won fewer electoral votes. In 2016, Hillary Clinton won the popular vote by over 3 million votes, but she lost the election to Donald Trump because he won more electoral votes.

These results are deeply troubling. They show that the Electoral College can sometimes result in a president who does not have the support of the majority of the American people. This is a dangerous precedent that threatens the very foundation of our democracy.

The Electoral College also creates an incentive for candidates to focus their attention on a handful of swing states, while ignoring the needs of the rest of the country. This is because the Electoral College system awards all of a state's electoral votes to the candidate who wins the popular vote in that state. This means that a candidate can win the presidency by carrying just a few large states, even if they lose the popular vote overall.

This is not a fair or representative system. It gives too much power to a small number of states, and it ignores the needs of the majority of the American people.

The National Popular Vote Interstate Compact is a bipartisan solution to the problem of the Electoral College. Under this compact, states would agree to award their electoral votes to the winner of the national popular vote. If enough states join the compact, it would effectively abolish the Electoral College and ensure that the president is elected by the majority of the American people.

I urge you to support the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. It is time to abolish the Electoral College and elect our president by popular vote.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

This could lead to a situation where a candidate only needs to win a few key swing states to secure the presidency, rather than having to win over a majority of voters across the country. On the other hand, under the Electoral College system, a candidate must win the support of a majority of electors, which means that they must have the support of a majority of voters in multiple states. This ensures that the president is truly elected by the people, rather than just a few key swing states.

Additionally, the Electoral College system encourages candidates to campaign across the entire country, rather than just focusing on a few key swing states. This is because in order to win the presidency, a candidate must not only win the support of their own party's voters, but also win over voters from the opposing party. This means that candidates are more likely to spend time and resources campaigning in states that they may not have previously considered important, which can help to ensure that the president is truly elected by the people, rather than just a few key swing states.

Finally, the Electoral College system provides a level of certainty in the election process. While there have been disputes over the outcome of Electoral College votes in the past, these disputes are relatively rare. In contrast, disputes over the outcome of popular vote totals could be much more common, as the difference between the winner and loser could be very small. This could lead to prolonged legal battles and a lack of certainty in the election process, which could be detrimental to the country as a whole.

In conclusion, I strongly support the Electoral College as the current method of electing the President of the United States. Dear Mr. Senator, As you are most likely aware, the Electoral College is a longdebated, controversial process. I believe that it is in the best interest for the citizens of America that the Electoral College be abolished. Under the Electoral College system, voters do not vote for the president but rather for a slate of electorss who will vote for the president. Voters cannot control who the electorss vote for and it is not unheard of that any given electors may be "faithless" and refuse to vote for their party's candidate and instead cast their deciding vote for whomever they want. The people of the United States of America are speaking up. According to a gallop poll conducted shortly after Al Gore won the popular vote but lost the presidency in 2000, over 60% a majority of voters prefer to have a direct election over an election through the Electoral College.

Bush Vs. Kerry election is rare, but nevertheless, it happened, are we going to wait until it happens again to make a change? We take pride in being a democracy, we take pride in living in such a place that was created by the people and for the people , but is the power really in the hands of the people? The power may be in the hands of the people, but only the 538 people who belong to the Electoral College. The system in place is flawed and the outcome can be manipulated to favor one political party over the other. In 1960, segregationists in Louisiana nearly successfully replaced the Democratic electorss with different electorss who would deceive the voters and then oppose Kennedy when voting.

Another con of The Electoral College is a dilemma that has to do with the number of electorsal votes given to each state. The Electoral College works in the same way that The House of Representatives does. The number of electorss alloted to each state is subjective to the population number of that state. Take a state such as California for example. California is alloted 55 electorss. States such as South Dakota and Alaska cant compete with the great power coming from the larger states. In the Congress, the Senate was created to balance it out, but there is nothing in place to balance the importance between large high density states and small low density states. Even more worrying is the situation in which there is a tie. In the case of a tie in the electorsal college, the election would be given to the House of Representatives, where state delegations would then have the deciding vote.

The Electoral College is outdated, unfair and impractical. The citizens of The United States are more than capable of making descisions for themselves and do not need electorss to make it for them. It is a nondemocratic method of selecting a president and should be abolished.

Thank You.

However, this compromise is no longer necessary. We now have the technology to conduct a national popular vote without any problems.

There are many arguments in favor of abolishing the Electoral College. First, it is undemocratic. The candidate who wins the most votes should be the President. Third, it is unfair to candidates who do not appeal to swing states. Candidates are forced to focus their campaigns on a few swing states, and they ignore the needs of the rest of the country.

Finally, the Electoral College does not force candidates to campaign all over the country. Candidates still focus their campaigns on a few swing states.

I disagree with the principal's decision that all students must participate in at least one extracurricular activity. While extracurricular activities provide many benefits, mandatory participation should not be required.

There are several reasons why participation should be a choice rather than a requirement. Not all students have the time or ability to take part in extracurriculars due to other commitments or limitations. Some students may need to focus their energy on academics in order to achieve academic goals. They may have jobs, family obligations, or other responsibilities outside of school that prohibit taking on additional commitments. Forcing participation could negatively impact their performance in class or personal lives. 

Additionally, different types of extracurricular activities suit different students. The choices should match individual interests, talents, and schedules. For example, an introverted student may not feel comfortable performing in a play but could enjoy contributing to the school newspaper. Making extracurriculars compulsory removes students' ability to select activities where they will thrive based on their own preferences. When done willingly, activities are more meaningful and the outcomes are better.

Finally, not all students have access to participate in activities due to financial or transportation constraints outside of their control. Requiring participation unfairly penalizes those without means regardless of desire or work ethic. This inequity could damage students' self-esteem and demotivate their engagement in school. 

In conclusion, while extracurriculars offer valuable learning experiences when chosen freely, mandatory participation deprives students of ownership over how they spend their time. It is preferable that these opportunities remain available to all on a voluntary basis so that each student can tailor involvement to best suit their own situation and foster achievement and well-being. The students' and the school's needs are usually best served when individual circumstances are respected and students are empowered to participate through their own autonomous decision making.

Car usage has been on the rise for decades, with more and more people relying on their cars for transportation. However, there are a number of advantages to limiting car usage, both for individuals and for the environment.

One of the main advantages of limiting car usage is that it can save money. Cars are expensive to purchase, maintain, and insure. In addition, driving a car costs money in terms of gas, parking, and tolls. If you can walk, bike, or take public transportation instead of driving, you can save a lot of money.

Another advantage of limiting car usage is that it can help you stay healthy. Driving can be stressful, and it can also lead to obesity and other health problems. If you walk, bike, or take public transportation instead of driving, you'll be getting more exercise and you'll be less likely to experience stress.

Limiting car usage can also help reduce pollution. Cars are one of the main sources of air pollution, and they contribute to climate change. If you can walk, bike, or take public transportation instead of driving, you'll be helping to improve air quality and reduce your impact on the environment.

Finally, limiting car usage can make your community a more pleasant place to live. When there are fewer cars on the road, it's easier to get around, the air is cleaner, and there's less noise pollution. If you want to make your community a better place to live, consider limiting your car usage.

Another way to limit car usage is to take public transportation. Many cities have excellent public transportation systems that can take you anywhere you need to go. If you live in a city with public transportation, consider using it instead of driving.

You can also limit car usage by carpooling. If you have to drive somewhere, consider carpooling with someone else who is going the same way. This will help to reduce the number of cars on the road and it will save you money. Finally, you can also limit car usage by telecommuting. If your job allows it, consider working from home instead of driving to the office. This will reduce your carbon footprint and it will give you more time to spend with your family and friends.

Limiting car usage can have a number of benefits for both individuals and for the environment. If you're looking to save money, improve your health, reduce pollution, or make your community a better place to live, consider limiting your car usage.

Online Learning: An Ineffective Teaching Method

With the emergence of modern technology in our everyday lives, it often seems logical that it should be integrated into our school systems.

Many schools allow children to take classes online through "distance learning" programs.

However, online learning is not nearly as effective as physical school at teaching children and giving them a solid understanding of the subject matter.

It allows students to fool around without restriction and encourages them not to attend school in the first place.

Furthermore, school should stay primarily uninvolved from the home life of a child.

Some think that it would be especially great for those who cannot physically attend school because of health reasons.

Those individuals should be focussing on recovering rather than their education.

Online learning is not nearly as effective at educating students.

At the school I attend, online courses are offered as a replacement for physical classroom courses.

From speaking to others that have taken online courses, they all view them as a nuisance that does not teach them anything comparable to taking an actual class at school.

All of the students who have taken them do not think they have really learned anything because of them.

This makes sense because of how easy it is to get distracted when on the computer.

Even students with good self control have difficulty sitting in on a virtual lecture when pressing the new tab button and opening YouTube would be simple.

For this reason, online classes will never be capable of matching the teaching capabilities of an actual learning environment, like school.

Aside form the evident issues of productivity and effectiveness of online education, home should be a place where school should stay primarily uninvolved.

Everyone looks forward to a returning home after a hard day of work or school.

If school primarily takes place at home, then students will associate their own safe place with hard work and frustration when it should be a place to decompress.

A separation between learning and relaxing locations is necessary for optimal learning conditions.

Many think that online schooling would be a good way to avoid kids having to attend school, especially for those who are not physically able to.

Online schooling may be useful for children who are to sick to attend school, however it does not provide any useful advantage to students who are capable of attending school normally.

Also, students who are not physically able to attend school for medical reasons should be focusing on recovering rather than schoolwork.

If online schooling is given as an option over normal education, it will allow more kids to slack off without the encouragement and motivation that a physical classroom provides.

It would also eliminate the beneficial seperation between school and home life.

Online learning is an ineffective teaching method.

I am writing to express my thoughts on the proposed policy change that would require students to have at least a B average in order to participate in sports and extracurricular activities. A B average mandate may also have unintended academic consequences. The pressure of such high-stakes grades could increase stress levels for some and prove counterproductive to learning. Students running the risk of losing activities may focus on grade requirements over comprehension. Those on the cusp of a B could lessen extra effort or give up entirely. 

Rather than an across-the-board change, a more balanced approach is needed. Maintaining minimum GPA standards is reasonable but setting the bar at B excludes many capable students. Eligibility could depend on individual progress or teachers’ feedback on effort instead of just final marks. Tutoring programs could help those striving for improvement. Most importantly, we must recognize the multifaceted ways all students can succeed and encourage their growth in both academics and leadership through experience.

In closing, while upholding academic performance is essential, banning participation for average work risks compromising student wellness and missing larger goals of development. A more nuanced policy considering each student’s full potential seems most aligned with our school’s educational mission. I hope these perspectives will be helpful as you consider options to balance challenge and support for our whole community.

Sincerely,

Dear Senator,

I am writing to you today to express my strong support for abolishing the Electoral College and electing the President of the United States by popular vote.

The Electoral College is an outdated system that is no longer representative of the American people. In the past, it made sense to have a system in which each state had a certain number of electors based on its population. However, that system is no longer necessary, and it actually prevents the voices of millions of Americans from being heard.

In the last two presidential elections, the candidate who won the popular vote lost the election. This is simply unacceptable in a democracy. The President should be the person who has the support of the majority of the people, not the person who can win the most swing states.

There are many reasons why the Electoral College is unfair. First, it gives more power to voters in small states than voters in large states. For example, a voter in Wyoming has more than three times the voting power of a voter in California. This is because each state has at least three electoral votes, regardless of its population.

Second, the Electoral College encourages candidates to focus on a few swing states and ignore the rest of the country. This is because the Electoral College gives all of a state's electoral votes to the winner of the popular vote in that state. This means that candidates can win the presidency by winning a narrow majority of the votes in a few key states, even if they lose the popular vote overall.

Third, the Electoral College is susceptible to fraud and abuse. There have been several cases in which faithless electors have voted for candidates other than the ones who won the popular vote in their state. This could happen again in the future, and it could throw the election into chaos.

Abolishing the Electoral College would be the fairest and most democratic way to elect the President of the United States. It would ensure that every vote counts, and it would give all Americans a voice in choosing their leader.

I urge you to support abolishing the Electoral College and electing the President by popular vote.

Sincerely,

Taking away these activities could actually have a negative impact on their academic performance. Every student learns differently, and extracurriculars provide an opportunity for learning skills and developing talents outside the classroom.

Restricting participation may discourage students from continuing to try their best if they face the risk of consequences from a single bad grade. 

Instead of requiring a B average, I think the present C average policy is fair while still reinforcing the importance of academic achievement. Students could be allowed to participate conditionally, with the requirement that they attend study sessions or work with teachers if their grades begin to drop below a C. This balanced approach supports students' well-being and continued involvement in school, while also challenging them to be responsible.

In closing, while raising standards is reasonable, an inflexible B average mandate risks doing more harm than good. I ask that you reconsider maintaining the current C average eligibility and explore alternative ways of motivating academic success that do not exclude students who are earnestly striving for improvement. In my opinion, self-made decisions and decisions made by people with more expertise and experience have their own advantages and disadvantages. In this essay, I will compare and contrast these two types of decisions and explore their implications.

Self-made decisions are those that individuals make on their own, without the guidance or input of others. While this type of decision-making can be empowering and give individuals a sense of control over their lives, it can also be risky and lead to suboptimal outcomes. For example, if a person is trying to decide on a career path, they may choose a field that they are passionate about but may not have the necessary skills or knowledge to succeed. This could lead to a lack of job satisfaction and financial stability.

On the other hand, decisions made by people with more expertise and experience can be beneficial as they have a deeper understanding of the subject matter and can provide valuable insights. For example, when it comes to investing in the stock market, it is important to seek advice from financial experts who have experience in the field. They can provide guidance on which stocks to buy and sell, and help individuals avoid costly mistakes. However, this type of decision-making can also be limiting as individuals may not have the freedom to make their own choices.

In conclusion, both self-made decisions and decisions made by people with more expertise and experience have their own advantages and disadvantages. While self-made decisions can be empowering and give individuals control over their lives, they can also be risky and lead to suboptimal outcomes. On the other hand, decisions made by people with more expertise and experience can be beneficial as they provide valuable insights, but can also be limiting as individuals may not have the freedom to make their own choices. Ultimately, it is important to consider the situation and weigh the pros and cons before making a decision.

The Electoral College has been established since the founding of our country. It is a system that has been tried and tested to work over the course of centuries. It should be upheld for it's ability to produce a solid outcome, and though it has the possibility of failing it's faults are not worse than the popular vote system, and that the Electoral College fosters a presidency campaign that appeals to multiple regions of the United States. This fair system allows representation of the people's will, just like the rest of our government does.

Faith in a certain outcome of the presidential election ensures that the vote has as little complications as possible, and is a reason the Electoral College is necessary. According to source one, "What Is The Electoral College?", each political party has it's own set of electors that equal the amount of congressional delegates per state. Usually each state has a "winner-take-all" method, so the presidential candidate that gets majority in your state will get all of the electors that represent their party, not just most of them. This is beneficicial to the outcome of the election becuase it makes the ability for a candiate to get majority vote much simpler. There is less of a possibility of a tie, or an outcome where no candidate wins. Source 3, "In Defense of the Electoral College: Five reasons to keep out despised method of choosing president", states that "even a very slight plurality in a state creates a landslide electoral-vote victory in that state..." , therefore allowing the candidate to secure all votes to their side, instead of having the votes divided on the line of majority rule, and causing rifts between Electoral College voters.

No system is perfect, and the Electoral College is not exempt from this. "The Indefensible Electoral College: Why even the best-laid defenses of the system are wrong", Source 2, argues that a term called 'disaster factor', or the possibility of immenent disaster due to the Electoral College system, is why the Electoral College system should be abolished. The passage uses individual instances, like the fact that in 1960, segrigationists in Lousiana nearly appointed Democratic electors that would vote against their candidate, or that in rare instances, "faithless" electoral voters would vote for the other side. These are strawman arguments, using specific instances to come to a conclusion that the whole system should be abolished. While the Electoral College system isn't perfect, neither is the popular vote system. The popular vote system has a higher chance of causing a tie between candidates, and it doesn't have a "winner-take-all" standard. In a tie, the vote would be given to the House of Representatives, which, according to source 2, "..can hardly be expected to reflect the will of the people..", as citizens often vote one party in for president and another for Congress.

In addition, the Electoral College fosters a more nationwide appeal for the candidate's campaign. Source 3 brings up the fact that no region in the United States has enough electoral votes to elect a president. The "winner-take-all" system further benefits this, because in order to win, candidates have to focus their attention on states where their majority vote is insecure. They will not focus on regions where they have essentially secured the majority rule and therefore secured all the electoral votes. In popular vote, they would have to focus extensively on those regions, as the few that are not in the majority would need convincing. Source 3 goes into detail as to why a regionally picked candidate is not a proper show of the will of the people. Self-improvement is an important and necessary part of life. It can be hard to know where to start, especially when it comes to finding the best approach. While there is no one-size-fits all answer, two of the most popular methods are improvisation and following a script when trying to be someone. These two methods have their own set of benefits and drawbacks, and understanding them can help us decide which is best for our own individual needs. 

Improvising when trying to be someone is a great way to achieve goals on the spot. It can help you think on your feet and allow you to be more creative in your approach and better adjust to unpredictable situations. A great example of this would be a public speaker. The ability to think quickly and remain strategic in one’s approach can be helpful in persuading an audience and having a greater impact. However, there is also the risk that if we do not know our subject matter well enough, the speech can go off the rails and lead to results that are less than ideal.

On the other hand, following a script can be very helpful for a number of situations. When someone is stuck in a rut, or trying something entirely new, following a step-by-step process can help them establish a foundation and develop their skills over time. This can be especially beneficial in contexts such as business or entrepreneuring, as if the individual is properly prepared, this can allow them to better anticipate obstacles and make better decisions in the long run. Of course, with this method, there is the risk of becoming overly reliant on a script and becoming dependent on it, leading to a lack of creative thinking. 

In conclusion, both improvisation and following a script can be valuable and helpful tools when pursuing self-improvement. It’s important to consider the context and end goals in order to determine which method best fits the individual, as well as how effective it is over time.

It should come as no surprise that the secret to scholarly success is to stay one step ahead of the competition. Recognizing this, many schools have opted to assign summer course work to ensure their students start the next year strong. However, they often face the dilemma over whether these assignments should be designed by teachers or by the students themselves. Despite the possibility of kids slacking off, student-driven summer work will prepare students for a future in their chosen field and ease the stressful workloads of both teachers and students alike.

The stress of a high school environment is all but increasing, and has been for decades. This trend has been documented extensively over the years, and all these studies sum up to high-schoolers, on average, being exhausted, overworked and overall unhappy on a daily basis. Teachers are not spared either, as they face the same struggles their students deal with day in and day out, often for no more than a substandard salary to say the least. Therefore, it makes sense for schools to do anything in their means to ease the burdens of a rigorous academic climate. One of the best ways to go about this would be to allot responsibilities of designing summer work from teachers to their students.

Another advantage of this proposition is that students will be able to take control of their own educational futures. The thought and effort they put into their summer work will directly manifest itself in their scores. Those who perform poorly will score poorly, whereas those who take it seriously will reap the rewards. This is the best way for teachers to measure the academic integrity of a class, allowing them to hone in on students who need assistance the most over the coming school year. As an added benefit, students will be pushed to learn other essential skills such as time management and independence which will certainly come into play later on in their lives.

Perhaps most important of all, students will have the opportunity to pursue an area of study of their choice. An individualized approach tailored for and by each student on their own is sure to make learning a more enjoyable and productive experience. In contrast, a standardized assignment designed to fulfill the needs and wants of each unique individual in a class at once amounts to nothing but stress, frustration and apathy towards what could have been an indispensable tool for students' future careers.

The advantages of a student-driven summer project far outweigh the potential pitfalls of such a program.

Those who would be inclined to laze their way out of assignments will find ways to avoid doing work no matter what, so why impede the success of the majority due to the inevitable actions of the few? Hopefully soon enough academic institutions will come to their senses and adopt such policies which provide unlimited benefit to all involved.
